module_title: Operation and Monitoring of Biogas Systems

lessons.title: Start-up Procedures for Anaerobic Digesters
lessons.body:
Starting a new biogas digester is like starting a fireâyou need the right materials and patience. First, ensure your digester is clean and leak-free. For a typical 6 cubic meter fixed-dome digester in Kenya, you'll need about 1,500 kg of fresh cow dung. Mix it with water in a 1:1 ratio to make a slurry. If cow dung isn't available, use pig or poultry manure, but avoid too much poultry litter as it can be too acidic. Add the slurry to the digester, filling it to about 80% capacity. The remaining space is for gas. Seal the digester immediately.

Temperature matters. In warm regions like Tanzania, the slurry will start producing gas in 2-3 days if the temperature is above 20Â°C. In cooler highlands, it may take 4-6 weeks. To speed up start-up, add a starter culture from an existing working digesterâabout 10% of the volume. If you don't have that, mix in some rumen fluid from a slaughtered cow. Keep the digester out of direct sunlight if possible, but insulate it if nights are cold.

Monitor gas production daily. The first gas may contain high carbon dioxide and won't burn well. Flush the gas line for a few minutes each day until you get a steady blue flame. This can take 1-2 weeks. Check for leaks using soapy water on all connections. If you smell rotten eggs (hydrogen sulfide), that's normal at start-up, but if it persists, add a small amount of iron filings to the slurry.

Don't feed the digester too much at first. Start with a small amount of manure dailyâabout 10 kg for a 6 mÂ³ digesterâand increase gradually over 2 weeks. Keep a record of what you add and when. If the digester becomes too acidic (pH below 6.5), stop feeding and add lime or wood ash to raise pH. With careful attention, your digester will be fully operational in 3-4 weeks.

lessons.title: Routine Monitoring Parameters: Temperature, pH, Gas Production, Gas Composition
lessons.body:
To keep your biogas system running well, you must check four key things regularly: temperature, pH, gas production, and gas composition. Use simple tools you can buy at any agricultural supply store. For temperature, a soil thermometer or a cheap digital thermometer works. Insert it into the slurry through the inlet or a dedicated port. The ideal range for mesophilic bacteria is 30-38Â°C. If it drops below 20Â°C, gas production slows down. In cold areas, consider a greenhouse cover over the digester.

pH is critical. You can use pH paper strips or a digital pH meter. The ideal pH is 6.8-7.4. If pH drops below 6.5, the digester is turning acidicâoften from too much food waste or sudden loading. Add a handful of wood ash or lime, and reduce feeding. If pH goes above 8.0, add more fresh manure. Check pH twice a week, always at the same time of day.

Gas production is measured by your gas meter or by how long it takes to fill a known volume. For a 6 mÂ³ digester, expect 0.5-1.5 mÂ³ of gas per day depending on feeding. If production drops, check for leaks, temperature, or feeding issues. Keep a daily log of gas pressure using a simple water manometer or a pressure gauge.

Gas composition: you can't easily measure methane percentage without a gas analyzer, but you can do a flame test. A good flame is blue and steady. If it's yellow or flickering, the methane content is lowâoften due to too much water or air in the system. Flush the gas line and check for leaks. Also, if the gas smells strongly of rotten eggs, the hydrogen sulfide level is high; this can corrode pipes. Install a hydrogen sulfide filter (iron sponge) if needed. Monitor these parameters weekly and record everything.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Data Analysis
lessons.body:
Good records are the backbone of a successful biogas system. Without them, you're guessing. Use a simple notebook or a chalkboard kept near the digester. Record daily: date, amount and type of feed (in kg), water added (in liters), temperature (Â°C), pH, gas pressure (in cm of water), and any observations (smell, color, foam). Also note when you desludge or repair. For a small farm, a 5-minute daily entry is enough.

Once a week, review your records. Look for patterns. For example, if you fed 20 kg of cow dung on Monday and gas pressure dropped on Tuesday, you might be overfeeding. If pH drops after adding leftover ugali (maize meal), that feed is too acidicâreduce it. Use a simple graph: plot gas production against feed amount. You'll quickly see the ideal feeding rate for your digester.

Data analysis doesn't need a computer. Calculate averages: total gas produced per week divided by 7 gives daily average. Compare weeks. If gas production falls by more than 20% from one week to the next, investigate. Check temperature first, then pH, then feeding. Also track costs: how much you spend on feed, water, and repairs. Compare that to savings on cooking gas or electricity. Many farmers in Uganda find they save 30-50% on energy costs after biogas.

Keep records for at least one year. This helps you plan for seasonal changesâfor example, in the dry season, water may be scarce, so you might need to adjust feeding. Share your records with extension officers or other farmers. In Kenya, the Kenya National Biogas Programme offers training on record keeping. A simple template can be downloaded from their website. Remember: if you don't write it down, it didn't happen.

lessons.title: Feeding Schedule and Organic Loading Management
lessons.body:
Feeding your digester is like feeding a cowâtoo little and it starves, too much and it gets sick. The key is consistency. For a 6 mÂ³ fixed-dome digester, a good starting point is 20-30 kg of fresh cow dung per day, mixed with an equal amount of water. If you use pig manure, use 15-20 kg because it's richer. Poultry litter is very strongâuse only 5-10 kg per day and mix with water well. Never feed more than the digester can handle; overflow will kill the bacteria.

Create a feeding schedule. Feed at the same time each day, preferably in the morning. This helps maintain stable conditions. If you miss a day, don't double the next dayâjust resume normal feeding. For best results, pre-mix the manure with water in a mixing pit before adding to the inlet. This prevents clogging and ensures even distribution. If you add food waste (like vegetable peels), chop it finely and limit it to 10% of the total feed. Too much food waste makes the slurry acidic.

Organic loading rate (OLR) is the amount of volatile solids (VS) per cubic meter of digester per day. For a small digester, aim for 0.5-1.5 kg VS/mÂ³/day. Cow dung has about 12-15% VS. So for a 6 mÂ³ digester, 20 kg of cow dung gives about 2.4-3 kg VS, which is 0.4-0.5 kg VS/mÂ³/dayâsafe. If you double that, you risk acidification. Monitor pH and gas production to adjust. If gas production drops and pH falls, reduce feed by half for a few days.

In hot weather, bacteria work faster, so you can feed slightly more. In cold weather, reduce feeding. During the rainy season, manure may be wateryâuse less water in the mix. Always keep a reserve of dry manure for times when fresh manure is scarce. And never feed your digester with soapy water, bleach, or antibioticsâthese kill the bacteria.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Operational Problems
lessons.body:
Even well-run digesters have problems. Here are the most common ones and how to fix them. First, no gas or low gas. Check for leaks firstâbrush soapy water on all pipes, valves, and the dome. Bubbles mean a leak; seal with silicone or replace the part. If no leaks, check temperature: if below 20Â°C, insulate the digester or add warm water. If pH is below 6.5, add wood ash (a handful per day) and stop feeding for 2 days. If pH is above 8.0, add fresh manure. Also, ensure you're not overfeedingâreduce feed by half for a week.

Second, gas burns poorly (yellow flame or flickers). This means low methane. Often caused by too much water in the gas lineâinstall a water trap and drain it. Or air entering through leaks. Fix leaks and flush the line. If the gas smells strongly of rotten eggs, hydrogen sulfide is high; add iron filings to the slurry or install a filter. If the flame is blue but small, you may have a clogged burnerâclean it with a wire brush.

Third, scum or crust forms on the slurry surface. This blocks gas from escaping. Break it up with a long stick or paddle. To prevent it, chop feed finely and avoid fibrous materials like straw. If the crust is thick, remove it manually through the inlet. Fourth, the digester overflows. This means you're adding too much. Stop feeding for a day, and check if the outlet is blocked. If the outlet pipe is clogged, clear it with a plumber's snake.

Fifth, pH crashes suddenly (below 6.0). This is an emergency. Add a bucket of lime or wood ash mixed with water, and stop feeding for 3 days. Then resume with half feed. Sixth, foam in the gas line. This happens when the slurry is too thinâadd less water to the feed. Also, check for detergent contamination. Finally, if the digester produces gas but it won't burn at all, the gas may be mostly carbon dioxide. Flush the system and check for air leaks. If problems persist, consult a biogas technician.

lessons.title: Emergency Procedures and Shutdown Protocols
lessons.body:
Emergencies in biogas systems can be dangerous if not handled quickly. The most serious is a gas leak that causes an explosion or asphyxiation. If you smell gas strongly (rotten eggs or a sweet smell), do not light a match or turn on any electrical switch. Open all doors and windows if indoors. Evacuate everyone, especially children and animals. Shut off the main gas valve if you can do so safely. Ventilate the area for at least 30 minutes. Then find the leak using soapy waterânever a flame. If the leak is in the dome, it may need professional repair.

If the digester overflows or bursts, it can release a large volume of slurry, which is corrosive and can burn skin. Wear gloves and boots. Contain the spill with soil or sand, and keep people away. If the slurry gets into a water source, notify local authorities immediately. For a fire in the gas line, shut off the gas supply and use a dry chemical fire extinguisher. Never use water on a gas fire. If you can't control it, call the fire brigade.

Shutdown protocols: if you need to stop the digester for repairs or because you're moving, you must do it properly. First, stop feeding for 2 weeks to let the bacteria consume remaining organic matter. Then, open the gas valve to release all gas safelyâdo this outdoors. Once gas pressure is zero, you can open the digester. Remove the slurry and store it as fertilizer (it's excellent for crops). Clean the digester with water, but don't use chemicals. If you plan to restart later, keep some slurry as inoculum in a sealed container.

For a permanent shutdown, after emptying, fill the digester with water to prevent cracks, or leave it dry but sealed. Never leave a digester openâit can collect rainwater and breed mosquitoes. Always have an emergency plan: post phone numbers for a biogas technician, fire service, and local health clinic near the digester. Train all family members on what to do in case of a leak or fire. Practice a drill once a year.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of fresh cow dung to water when preparing slurry for a new digester?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 ratio by volume is standard for proper digestion and flow.

quiz.q: How long does it typically take for a biogas digester to start producing gas in warm regions (above 20Â°C)?
quiz.explanation: In warm conditions, bacteria are active and gas production can begin within 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What should you do if the first gas produced does not burn well?
options: B) Flush the gas line daily until it burns blue
quiz.explanation: Initial gas has high CO2; flushing helps remove it until methane content is high enough.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: Methanogenic bacteria thrive best at a neutral pH between 6.8 and 7.4.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure gas pressure in a biogas system?
quiz.explanation: A water manometer measures the pressure of gas in the system.

quiz.q: What does a yellow or flickering flame indicate about biogas quality?
quiz.explanation: A yellow flame indicates incomplete combustion due to low methane and high CO2.

quiz.q: How often should you record monitoring parameters in a biogas system?
quiz.explanation: Daily records help detect trends and problems early.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily feed for a 6 mÂ³ digester using cow dung?
quiz.explanation: 20-30 kg of cow dung mixed with equal water is a safe starting point for a 6 mÂ³ digester.

quiz.q: What is the ideal organic loading rate for a small biogas digester?
quiz.explanation: 0.5-1.5 kg volatile solids per cubic meter per day is optimal for small digesters.

quiz.q: What should you do if the digester pH drops below 6.5?
options: B) Add wood ash or lime and reduce feeding
quiz.explanation: Wood ash or lime raises pH, and reducing feed prevents further acidification.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be added to a biogas digester?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water contains chemicals that kill anaerobic bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check if gas production drops suddenly?
quiz.explanation: Leaks are a common cause of sudden gas loss and should be checked first.

quiz.q: How can you test for gas leaks in a biogas system?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water applied to joints will bubble if there is a leak.

quiz.q: What causes a crust to form on the slurry surface?
quiz.explanation: Fibrous materials like straw float and form a crust that traps gas.

quiz.q: What is the emergency procedure if you smell a strong gas leak indoors?
options: A) Light a match to find the leak
D) Add water to the digester
quiz.explanation: Evacuate immediately, ventilate, and avoid any ignition sources.

quiz.q: What should you do before opening a digester for repairs?
options: B) Stop feeding for 2 weeks and release all gas
quiz.explanation: Stopping feed and releasing gas ensures safety by reducing methane and pressure.

quiz.q: How often should you check the pH of the digester slurry?
options: D) Only when gas production drops
quiz.explanation: Twice weekly checks help catch acidification early without excessive monitoring.

quiz.q: What is a good source of starter culture for a new digester?
options: B) Rumen fluid from a cow
quiz.explanation: Rumen fluid contains active anaerobic bacteria that jump-start digestion.

quiz.q: What does a blue, steady flame indicate?
quiz.explanation: A blue flame shows good methane content and proper combustion.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily feed for a 6 mÂ³ digester using pig manure?
quiz.explanation: Pig manure is richer than cow dung, so 15-20 kg per day is sufficient.

quiz.q: How can you increase pH if it is too low?
options: B) Add wood ash or lime
quiz.explanation: Wood ash and lime are alkaline and safely raise pH.

quiz.q: What should you do if the digester overflows?
options: B) Stop feeding for a day and check outlet
quiz.explanation: Overflow means overfeeding or blockage; stop feed and clear outlet.

quiz.q: What is a sign of high hydrogen sulfide in biogas?
quiz.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide has a distinct rotten egg odor.

quiz.q: How can you reduce hydrogen sulfide in biogas?
options: A) Add iron filings to slurry
quiz.explanation: Iron reacts with sulfide to form harmless iron sulfide.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a water trap in a gas line?
quiz.explanation: Water traps collect condensate that would otherwise block gas flow.

quiz.q: What should you do if the gas line is clogged with foam?
options: A) Add more water to feed
B) Reduce water in feed and check for detergent
quiz.explanation: Foam often results from too thin slurry or detergent contamination.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of biogas system operation?
options: A) To show off to neighbors
B) To identify trends and optimize performance
C) To increase gas production instantly
quiz.explanation: Records help detect problems and fine-tune feeding and maintenance.

quiz.q: What is the recommended frequency for reviewing biogas records?
quiz.explanation: Weekly reviews allow timely adjustments based on patterns.

quiz.q: What should you do with the slurry removed during shutdown?
options: D) Put it in a river
quiz.explanation: Digestate is a nutrient-rich organic fertilizer.

quiz.q: What is the first step in an emergency shutdown of a biogas system?
options: B) Stop feeding and release gas safely
quiz.explanation: Stopping feed and releasing gas reduces risk before any repair.
